# Mail

Three-pane conversation view over the same MOTE substrate as everything else in Envoir — mail is
simply MOTEs of `kind = mail`, designed to default to the metadata-private `private` transport
tier (see [Privacy & threat model](#privacy)); today only the `fast` (direct) tier actually
runs — see [Roadmap](#roadmap).

![Mail — three-pane inbox](assets/screens/mail-dark.png)

## The layout

- **Left rail** — folders (Inbox, Sent, Drafts, Snoozed, Archive, Spam, Trash) and your color
  labels, each with an unread count.
- **Middle pane** — the conversation list for whichever folder or label is selected. Search (the
  top-bar box, or `/`) filters this list live.
- **Right pane** — the open conversation, threaded, newest message expanded.

## Reading and triaging mail

Click a conversation in the middle pane to open it. From the reading pane or the list row you can:

- **Star** it (the star icon, or `s`) to flag it for later.
- **Archive** (`e`) or **delete** (`#`) — archived mail leaves the inbox but isn't gone; deleted
  mail goes to Trash first.
- **Snooze** (`b` or `h`, or the clock icon) — pick "later today," "tomorrow," or "next week" and
  the thread disappears from the inbox until then, reappearing with a `snoozed` chip in the
  meantime if you check the Snoozed folder.
- **Label** (`l`) — apply one of your color labels from the command menu that pops up.
- **Mark unread** (`u`) if you opened something by accident and want the bold-unread state back.
- Select multiple conversations with the checkbox (or `x`) to archive/mark-read/spam/delete in
  bulk — a bulk action bar replaces the list header the moment anything is selected.

Every keyboard shortcut is listed in-app via `?` (or Settings → Keyboard shortcuts).

## What the badges on a conversation mean

- A **verified ✓** badge next to a sender's name means you've checked their
  [safety number](#identity#safety-numbers-verifying-a-contacts-key) — see [Identity](#identity).
- A small **path badge** (shield, bolt, or bridge icon) on the row shows how that message arrived
  — pure-mesh private tier, pure-mesh fast tier, or gateway-touched. Click it to expand the full
  transport-path graph in the reading pane. See
  [Transport & provenance](#transport-traceability) for exactly what that graph can and can't
  show you.
- A **legacy-origin** chip marks any message that arrived through the
  [gateway](#self-hosting) rather than pure-mesh — meaning it was plaintext at that gateway
  before it reached the mesh. A pure-mesh message never carries this chip, because the protocol
  requires a gateway attestation for any legacy-origin mail, and a message with none provably
  never touched one.
- An **invite** chip means the message carries a calendar invitation — see
  [Calendar](#calendar).

## Inspecting a message — the MOTE inspector

Every message you send or receive is a **MOTE**: a signed, encrypted, content-addressed object
with three nested layers. Click the shield/lock icon on an open message to open the **MOTE
inspector**, which shows all three, live, for that specific message:

![MOTE inspector — the three sealed layers of a message](assets/screens/inspector-dark.png)

- **Outer** — what the mixnet and relays see: an onion-wrapped, constant-length packet, sender
  hidden. Even your own client only knows the tier (private/fast) and, for a group, the fan-out.
- **Envelope** — signed for authenticity; the content-addressed `id` (a hash of the ciphertext),
  the recipient, the message kind, and the crypto suite in use.
- **Payload** — the MLS/HPKE-encrypted content: real sender, subject, and body, decrypted here
  because you're the recipient viewing your own mailbox. The signature length shown is a genuine
  Ed25519 signature over that content.

This is the clearest way to see, concretely, *why* Envoir calls a message private — each layer
really does hide more than the last from anyone who isn't you.

## How delivery works

Mail addressed to a DMTAP identity resolves `name@domain` to a key (see [Identity](#identity)),
is sealed as a MOTE, and is designed to travel the mixnet by default — see
[Architecture](#architecture#message-flow) for the full sequence and
[Roadmap](#roadmap) for why only the `fast` tier is real today (the onion-wrap's mix
cryptography is a structural BLAKE3 stand-in, not yet the real Sphinx construction). Mail addressed
to a legacy address (`@gmail.com` and the like) is handed to a [gateway](#self-hosting), which is
the only component in the whole system that speaks SMTP and the only one that isn't content-blind.

## Client protocols

One MOTE store, projected through several protocol front-ends so existing tools work unchanged —
**JMAP** natively, plus **IMAP/POP3/SMTP-submission** and **CalDAV/CardDAV** compatibility served
by the optional gateway. If you'd rather point Thunderbird, Apple Mail, or a phone's built-in mail
app at Envoir instead of using the web client, see
[JMAP/IMAP/CalDAV client setup](#client-setup) for the full walkthrough.

## Calendar & contacts

Not separate central services — additional MOTE kinds stored on the same node, end-to-end
encrypted, synced across your device cluster, and shared/invited via the same MLS groups as
everything else. See [Calendar](#calendar) and [Contacts](#contacts), now at parity with Mail
and Chat in the web client.

## What's real vs. simulated today

MOTE construction, signing, and the inspector's three-layer breakdown above are real code running
on real (if demo) message data. Network delivery — actually carrying a MOTE across the mesh or
mixnet to another node — is a clearly-labeled in-browser simulation in this reference client (the
production path compiles the Rust protocol core to WASM and speaks to a real node over libp2p
instead). See [Roadmap](#roadmap) for the project-wide real-vs-simulated line, and
[`client/README.md`](https://github.com/vul-os/envoir/blob/main/client/README.md) for the client's own exact table.
